title: Margin debt hits a record, and retail is trading with borrowed money
dek: Margin debt at US brokerages now exceeds total US credit card debt, and a leveraged ETF crash in Korea forced the liquidation of 360,000 accounts, most of them belonging to people under 35.
why: Two Indicators stitched together. The first half on Korea's leverage blowup has concrete mechanics and numbers; the second half on sports betting is thin on information, so you can listen to just the first half.
who: Investors and finance professionals watching retail leverage, brokerage risk controls and regulatory moves; people building consumer finance or betting compliance products also get a Colorado regulatory sample.
skip: The sports betting half (from 11:16) is thin on information; you can listen to just the Korea leverage blowup half.

points.h: Margin debt has passed credit card debt
points.body: Total margin borrowing in US stocks has hit a record, over $1.5 trillion, 50% higher than a year ago. A more intuitive comparison: total margin debt in the US brokerage system now exceeds total US credit card debt. In other words, more money is borrowed to trade stocks than is owed on credit cards. Making money with other people's money is great, until the market falls — the loan and the interest still have to be paid. Yale finance professor Heather Tewks says that when a stock falls too far, investors have only two choices: sell the stock to repay the loan, or put more money into the margin account.

points.h: India gave academics a natural experiment
points.body: Heather Tewks and her co-authors chose to study India because Indian regulators were friendly to scholars when designing the rules: which stocks can be bought on margin and which cannot is separated by a clear line. That creates a natural experiment to test whether margin trading really causes market instability. The conclusion is yes — margin does play a role, especially during financial crises. There is an amplification effect on the way down: the basket of margin-eligible stocks falls significantly more than the basket of non-margin-eligible stocks. Many margin investors are forced to sell holdings to repay loans, and that forced selling amplifies the overall losses.

points.h: Korea turned leveraged ETFs into a national game
points.body: The same mechanism just played out in Korea. Investors piled into SK Hynix and Samsung, the two companies making memory chips for AI data centers that dominate the Korean stock market. Fidelity global macro director Yurian Timmer describes it this way: semiconductor earnings tripled over the past year, everything felt like it was on fast-forward, a boom-bust cycle amplified across multiple dimensions. Earlier this year Korea legalized single-stock leveraged ETFs — they look like ordinary ETFs on the outside, but inside they hold leverage, futures and various financial tricks to magnify gains, and losses are magnified just the same. Such products have been legal in the US since 2022, and Korea wanted to catch up. On some days these ETFs accounted for 20% of volume on Korean exchanges.

points.h: The fundamentals were fine, and the accounts still went to zero
points.body: Yurian Timmer's assessment of these instruments: ‘I call them weapons of self-destruction, and I don't understand why regulators approve these things.’ His pessimistic call was at least borne out in Korea: the Korean stock market's market cap fell as much as 40%. At the company level, memory chip demand is still forecast to be strong, but investors were no longer as excited, leveraged bets began to unwind, and margin traders were forced to sell. More than 3% of Korean adults received a margin call. Goldman Sachs estimates that about 360,000 brokerage accounts were forced to liquidate all holdings to repay debt, and Citi data shows most of those accounts belonged to people under 35. Yurian's summary: the fundamentals of these companies are perfectly fine, the problem is just that you leaned too far forward — with leverage you can lose your entire principal.

points.h: The Fed has a tool it hasn't touched in decades
points.body: In the US, margin debt is also at a historic high, and the Fed actually has a little-known duty: setting how much money investors must have in their own pockets to borrow a dollar. Back to the opening example — you have $50 and want to buy $100 of Apple stock; the Fed can say, be careful, the broker can only lend you $25 instead of $50. The Fed fiddled with this requirement in the years after the Great Depression, and that crash came after a surge in margin debt inflated a bubble. But Yurian thinks we are not yet at the panic point: during the 2000 dot-com bubble the rate of change in margin debt was 81%, today it is about 40%, much slower. He calls the current moment a yellow zone, not a panic point. The Fed has not touched this requirement since 1974, and when a reporter contacted its press office, no one was willing to respond on the record.

points.h: Spotting a bubble is easy, timing the pop is hard
points.body: Yurian Timmer thinks the Fed may be reluctant to intervene in margin trading for a simple reason: the Fed generally does not want to get mixed up in the stock market and bubbles, because it believes no one can predict these things. Greenspan called the Nasdaq a bubble back in 1996, and it ran for another four years. So the Fed is at least humble enough to know it cannot time these things. Spotting a forming bubble is easy; timing the pop is much harder — you do not want to shut down a party that might keep going for a long while.

points.h: A quarter of Gen Z treat sports betting as investing
points.body: The line between investing and gambling has blurred. Over the past year, more than half of Gen Z said they used money meant for investing to place sports bets. Sports betting ads keep promoting free bets like ‘deposit $5, get $300’, making betting look like easy money. Eight years after the federal sports betting ban was overturned, the effect on young people is only now showing up. In a recent survey, about a quarter of Gen Z said they see sports betting as a high-risk investment strategy, or a way to reach a goal faster. Dan Egan, vice president of behavioral science and investing at Betterment, says the danger is that we start treating a hobby as an investment — like people who collect cars, who honestly admit it is not about making money, it is a hobby.

points.h: Colorado chose to add friction for bettors
points.body: State governments are starting to respond to the negative effects of sports betting, including addiction. Colorado passed a new law making it the first state that allows sports betting to ban betting companies from sending customers mobile push notifications and texts — those ‘hey, looks like there's a game, want to bet’ reminders are gone. The bill also limits how many times a single customer can deposit in one day, capped at six. Co-sponsor and Democratic state senator Matt Ball says he is not trying to ban gambling — he has bet on sports himself and has been commissioner of a fantasy league for 15 years — but people in his district came to him about the issue, from a mother whose son came home from college and ran up $15,000 on a credit card in one night, to problem gambling experts nationally. Problem gambling is linked to more bankruptcies, loan defaults, domestic violence and suicide. Matt himself admits: we do not have any data, and to some extent we are guessing.

terms.def: Borrowing money from a broker to buy stocks, using your own funds as collateral, with losses and interest both magnified.
A broker demanding that an investor add money or sell holdings, otherwise forcibly liquidating positions to cover the loan.
An ETF that tracks a single stock and uses leverage and futures internally to magnify gains and losses.
A market for betting on the outcome of events, such as Polymarket and Kalshi, a different category from sports betting.
